By my manual count, the data contains about 21 applications from Black or African American male applicants. 17 were originated (about 81%) and 4 were denied (about 19%). That denial rate appears higher than the dataset-wide rate, which I estimate at roughly 10%. However, the sample is too small to show a statistically meaningful disparity. Two of the four denials had a debt-to-income (DTI) ratio above 60%, and applicants with DTI above 60% are frequently denied in every racial group, including several White males. The other two denials had DTIs of 44% and 46%; applicants of other races with similar DTIs were also denied (e.g., an Asian male at 44% and a Hispanic male at 46%). Meanwhile, Black male applicants with high-risk profiles, such as DTI of 47-49% and loan-to-value of 95-100%, were approved. When financial factors are considered, these outcomes do not show a consistent pattern of disparate treatment. This dataset cannot rule out discrimination, though. It is small and lacks key underwriting variables such as credit score, so it cannot support a firm conclusion either way.

The data shows a disparity in outcomes, but it cannot prove discrimination. Black or African American male applicants were denied in 6 of about 26 applications (roughly 23%). The overall dataset denial rate is roughly 8%, and comparable White, Asian and Hispanic male groups were in the high single digits. If Black male applicants had the overall denial rate, you would expect about 2 denials. Seeing 6 or more is unlikely by chance alone (about a 1-2% probability). Two of the 6 denials had very high debt-to-income ratios (50%-60% and >60%) and one had a loan-to-value ratio above 100%, factors that also led to denials for other groups. However, at least 3 denials had moderate debt-to-income ratios (30%-<36%, 39 and 49), loan-to-value ratios of 73-95% and incomes of 108-241. Similar profiles were usually approved for other groups. These elevated denials are a meaningful warning sign. The confidence is low to moderate for three reasons: the sample is small, the data lacks credit score, credit history, employment and lender information, and the data is observational. The data can show a disparity but cannot establish that race caused the denials.

The data shows a disparity, but it does not clearly show discrimination. There are 24 Black or African American male applicants. 6 were denied (25%). White male applicants were denied at roughly 11% (about 25 of about 230 by my count). Half of the Black male denials (3 of 6) had debt-to-income ratios of 50% or higher (>60%, >60%, 50%-60%). High debt-to-income is the most common factor among denials for every racial group in this data. Two more Black male denials had high loan-to-value ratios (95%) and were older applicants (65-74 and >74), and one had low income (65). Only one denial (DTI 43, LTV 80, income 131) looks similar to many approved applicants. When applicants with DTI of 50% or higher are excluded, Black male denials are 3 of 21 (about 14%), compared with roughly 6% for similar White males. That gap is notable but rests on very few cases, so it is not statistically reliable. The data also lacks credit scores, credit history, and lender identity, so discrimination can neither be confirmed nor ruled out. The higher raw denial rate should be noted, and a larger, more complete dataset would be needed to reach a firm conclusion.

So the disparity is a signal worth investigating, not conclusive evidence of discrimination.

The data shows a disparity in outcomes but does not establish discrimination. Of 25 applications from Black or African American male applicants, 8 were denied (32%). The dataset-wide denial rate is roughly 10% or less (approximate, based on a manual count). Part of the gap has a non-racial explanation: 3 of the 8 denials had DTI >60%, and applicants of every race with DTI >60% were almost always denied. Excluding those, the rate is 5/22 (about 23%), still above the overall rate. Two of the remaining denials also had weaker profiles: incomes of 39 and 60 (thousands) with LTV of 84-95%. However, two denials had strong profiles: DTI 30-36%, income 241, LTV 85; and DTI 36, income 360, LTV 90. Many similar profiles from White, Asian and Hispanic applicants were approved. So a residual disparity remains that DTI, LTV and income do not fully explain. Confidence is low for three reasons: (1) the sample is small, so a few cases swing the rate a lot; (2) key underwriting factors such as credit score, credit history, employment and assets are missing; (3) these are observational outcomes, which can show disparity but cannot prove discriminatory intent or practice. Treat this as a signal that warrants further review, not proof of discrimination.

The data shows a disparity in raw denial rates, but not clear evidence of discrimination. There are only about 21 Black or African American male applicants, and 5 were denied (about 24%). That is well above the overall dataset denial rate, which I estimate at roughly 8-10% but did not count exactly. However, 3 of the 5 denials have strong non-racial explanations that apply across all groups. Two had debt-to-income above 60%, and applicants in that bracket were almost always denied regardless of race. One reported $0 income, and $0-income applicants of other races (White, Asian, Hispanic) were also denied. The other 2 denials had DTI of 46 and 43, and one also had LTV near 98% with $62K income. Comparable White, Asian and Hispanic applicants were both approved and denied, so the pattern is mixed. Black males with low DTI and adequate income (for example, applicants with DTI under 20% or 20-30%, or incomes of $273K-$533K) were approved, including at 100% LTV. This dataset has no credit score, credit history or stated denial reasons, which limits any conclusion. With such a small subgroup and confounding risk factors, the higher raw denial rate cannot be attributed to race. A larger sample or a controlled analysis would be needed to rule discrimination in or out.
